reasoning.scenario: A sixth-form college has 300 Year 12 and 200 Year 13 pupils. The research question compares study time across year groups. Complete year-group registers exist. The team can sample 50 pupils.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise year-group representation while selecting pupils randomly.

reason: A proportional selection of 30 Year 12 and 20 Year 13 pupils, randomly chosen from each list, represents both groups in the design.
Taking the first 50 people in the library is guaranteed to include both year groups.
A proportional split is impossible when each year group has its own register.
limitation: Some randomly chosen pupils may not respond, and proportional allocation does not guarantee a representative realised sample.
Every individual would have the same chance of selection regardless of group size.
Random selection means no nonresponse bias can arise.
improvement: Plan follow-ups for nonrespondents and explain how response rates differ between year groups.
Replace each nonrespondent with the nearest friend.
Keep the first 50 volunteers and still call it stratified random.

reasoning.model: I would use stratified random sampling: split pupils by year group, allocate 30 and 20 places, and randomly select different pupils within each register. This matches the study's focus on comparing years. Nonresponse could still distort the results, so I would follow up and report response rates by year.
reasoning.tradeoff: A census would also supply both groups, but it may not be practical with limited time.

evidence.label: Aim
evidence.text: Compare study time between Year 12 and Year 13.

evidence.label: Frame
evidence.text: Complete registers for 300 Year 12 and 200 Year 13 pupils.

coaching.method: Separate year groups, then choose pupils randomly within each to avoid convenience-based selection.
coaching.reason: The population split is 60:40, so 30 from Year 12 and 20 from Year 13 gives proportional allocation.
coaching.limitation: Group proportions in the selection design do not guarantee response; nonrespondents can affect the final data.
coaching.improvement: Following up selected nonrespondents and checking year-specific response rates addresses this concrete risk.

method.quota: Quota targets do not require random choice within groups; complete registers permit stratified random selection.
method.opportunity: An available group may omit a year or skew its share, despite the complete registers.

reason.1: The library queue is a convenience group, with no guarantee of coverage across both year groups.
reason.2: Separate registers make proportional sampling easier, not impossible.

limitation.1: With a correctly implemented proportional random sample, individual inclusion probabilities can be equal; this is not the principal limitation here.
limitation.2: Random selection does not make pupils respond to a questionnaire.

improvement.1: Replacing nonrespondents with friends changes the random selection process and adds potential bias.
improvement.2: Selecting volunteers is not equivalent to drawing names randomly from each year-group list.

reasoning.scenario: A quality inspector needs 20 items from a batch of 200 stored in an ordered register. The order is not linked to any repeating production pattern.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise a quick, evenly spread sample with an available ordered list.

reason: A random start in positions 1–10, followed by every tenth item, spreads the sample through the batch.
Choosing the first 20 items is random because they are in a list.
A quota guarantees every individual item has the same chance of selection.
limitation: If the ordering actually has a ten-item cycle, this design could be distorted.
A random start automatically removes all possible ordering effects.
This method requires interviewing volunteers.
improvement: Check the register for hidden periodic patterns before sampling.
Remove the random starting position to save time.
Select only items from the first box.

reasoning.model: I would use systematic sampling with interval 200/20=10 and a random start from 1 to 10, then take every tenth item. It is efficient and covers the ordered batch. A hidden ten-item production cycle could bias selection, so I would first inspect how items are ordered.
reasoning.tradeoff: Simple random selection could also be defensible if the complete frame is easy to number.

evidence.label: Ordering
evidence.text: No repeating production pattern is currently known.

coaching.method: A systematic design uses the existing ordered list, with a random starting position.
coaching.reason: The interval is 200 ÷ 20 = 10; randomly start at 1–10 and then take every tenth item.
coaching.limitation: A hidden ten-item cycle could align with the interval and repeatedly select one phase.
coaching.improvement: Checking the sequence for periodicity directly addresses the risk created by the selection interval.

method.opportunity: Picking readily available items is not a systematic, evenly spread draw from the list.
method.quota: Group targets are unnecessary; the study concerns items from one complete ordered register.

reason.1: The first 20 entries are a fixed block rather than a randomised systematic draw.
reason.2: Quota sampling does not guarantee equal individual selection probabilities.

limitation.1: A random starting point does not remove periodicity when the interval matches the cycle.
limitation.2: Inspecting stored parts does not involve recruiting volunteer survey participants.

improvement.1: Removing the random start destroys the probability element of this systematic procedure.
improvement.2: Sampling one box only risks leaving the rest of the batch uncovered.

reasoning.scenario: A student has twenty minutes at a school sports event to hear quick impressions from attendees. There is no attendee register and results are explicitly described as exploratory.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise feasibility and be honest about what the evidence supports.

reason: Approaching available eligible attendees is possible without constructing a complete sampling frame.
A sample at one entrance is guaranteed to represent every spectator.
The easiest way to ensure proportional strata is to ask only friends.
limitation: People present at that entrance and time may differ from all attendees.
No one can refuse to answer a convenient survey.
The method requires a randomly chosen position within every interval.
improvement: Try several entrances and time periods, then describe the coverage limitation.
Claim the results apply to all local residents.
Ignore any differences between available volunteers and absent spectators.

reasoning.model: For quick exploratory feedback I would use opportunity sampling, asking eligible attendees who are available. The responses may overrepresent people at that entrance and time, so I would visit several locations and make the limitation explicit.
reasoning.tradeoff: If a full list became available and generalisation mattered, a probability-based method would be preferable.

evidence.label: Purpose
evidence.text: Quick exploratory feedback at a sports event.

coaching.method: Opportunity sampling is workable for exploratory impressions when only available attendees can be reached.
coaching.reason: Recruiting available eligible attendees fits the short time limit and does not pretend to be random.
coaching.limitation: Only attendees passing the location at that time can respond, so views may be systematically different.
coaching.improvement: Covering several entrances and times improves variety, but it still does not create a random sample.

method.simple-random: Simple random sampling would need an eligible frame and random selection, neither of which is available.
method.stratified: Stratified random sampling requires defined strata and random selections within them.

reason.1: A single entrance is a selective location; it does not guarantee representation of spectators.
reason.2: Friends are a convenience group, not a proportional random selection from strata.

limitation.1: Respondents may decline, regardless of whether recruitment is convenient.
limitation.2: Random starting positions belong to systematic sampling, not opportunity sampling.

improvement.1: The attendees do not support an inference to all residents of the area.
improvement.2: Ignoring who was absent hides the most important limitation of the design.

reasoning.scenario: A survey team needs responses from 40 commuters and 60 non-commuters this week. No complete list of people exists, but fieldworkers can recruit in several locations.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise meeting the two specified group targets with limited resources.

reason: Set the two group quotas and recruit eligible available respondents until each is full.
Choose only the first 100 people, ignoring how many are commuters.
Random-number generation is possible without any sampling frame.
limitation: Within each quota, the available respondents are not randomly chosen, so selection bias can remain.
The sample is guaranteed to be representative because it has group targets.
A systematic sampling interval removes nonresponse.
improvement: Recruit at multiple sites and times and report that within-group selection was non-random.
Call the result stratified random without changing recruitment.
Only recruit near a commuter station during rush hour.

reasoning.model: Quota sampling fits the fieldwork constraint. I would set targets of 40 commuters and 60 non-commuters and recruit eligible respondents until each quota is filled. Selection within groups is non-random, which may bias the results; I would vary locations and times and report this limitation.
reasoning.tradeoff: Stratified random sampling would usually be stronger for generalisation, but needs usable frames within strata.

evidence.label: Time
evidence.text: All fieldwork must be completed this week.

evidence.label: Frame
evidence.text: No complete list exists; multiple recruitment sites are available.

coaching.method: Quota sampling can meet category totals through non-random recruitment without a population list.
coaching.reason: The interviewer can approach eligible people until each preset group total is filled.
coaching.limitation: Within-group convenience recruitment can distort opinions even if the quotas are met.
coaching.improvement: Varying site and time broadens coverage while honestly retaining the non-random limitation.

method.systematic: Without a complete ordered frame, a systematic interval cannot be applied to the target population.
method.simple-random: Generating numbers cannot identify people equally from a missing population frame.

reason.1: The first 100 volunteers need not meet either quota.
reason.2: Random numbers alone are not a procedure without defined sampling units and a complete frame.

limitation.1: Group totals are not evidence that individuals within groups were randomly chosen.
limitation.2: A regular interval cannot remove bias caused by nonresponse.

improvement.1: Changing the name does not turn non-random quota recruitment into stratified random sampling.
improvement.2: A single commuter station at rush hour undercovers non-commuters and other times.

reasoning.scenario: A club has 120 members on a complete up-to-date register. It wants to ask 15 members about a change to meeting times without focusing on any subgroup.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise a probability sample from the complete list.

reason: Number all 120 members and select 15 different integers randomly, ignoring repeats.
Ask whichever 15 members next arrive, calling the method random.
Allocate equal quotas even though no group is relevant.
limitation: A particular subgroup can be underrepresented by chance despite random selection.
Random selection removes any possible nonresponse or measurement error.
A sampling frame prevents any member from declining the survey.
improvement: Check response rates and follow up sampled members; avoid claiming guaranteed representativeness.
Replace difficult-to-contact members with friends.
Select the same number twice if it is generated twice.

reasoning.model: A simple random sample is suitable with this complete register: number members 1–120 and generate random integers, ignoring repeats until 15 members are chosen. The realised sample may still be unbalanced or have nonresponse, so I would follow up and acknowledge these limits.
reasoning.tradeoff: If subgroup comparisons became important, stratified random sampling could be preferable.

evidence.label: Frame
evidence.text: A complete, up-to-date register of 120 club members.

coaching.method: With a complete member register and no subgroup requirement, simple random selection is straightforward.
coaching.reason: Unique labels from 1 to 120 and ignoring repeated random draws produce 15 distinct members.
coaching.limitation: A random sample can still contain an atypical mix by chance, and some people may not respond.
coaching.improvement: Checking responses and following up selected members helps address nonresponse without replacing random draws with friends.

method.quota: Quota sampling is unnecessary without meaningful categories and gives no random-selection guarantee.
method.opportunity: The next arrivals are conveniently accessible, not a random draw of all 120 members.

reason.1: Who arrives next depends on availability rather than a valid random selection procedure.
reason.2: Artificial equal quotas do not help when no subgroup comparison is required.

limitation.1: Random selection cannot prevent nonresponse or incorrect measurements.
limitation.2: A list identifies potential respondents; it does not force them to take part.

improvement.1: Friends are a non-random replacement and can create selection bias.
improvement.2: Keeping repeated labels gives fewer than 15 distinct members.

reasoning.scenario: A school intends to investigate travel habits among boarding and day pupils. Its full register identifies both categories, and both must appear in approximately their population proportions.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise category coverage and a defensible selection procedure.

reason: Allocate places in proportion to boarding/day numbers, then randomly draw distinct names within each group.
Recruit boarding pupils outside one dormitory and day pupils by the main gate.
Use every kth name from a list sorted by boarding status without checking its ordering.
limitation: Whole-number proportional allocations may need adjustment to total n, and selected pupils can still fail to respond.
A complete register guarantees everyone will complete the questionnaire.
Random sampling guarantees the sample's realised proportions in every other characteristic.
improvement: Check final allocations add up and plan follow-up contact across both groups.
Allow each group allocation to be rounded up even if the total exceeds n.
Replace random within-group draws with the first available pupils.

reasoning.model: I would use stratified random sampling: divide the full register into boarding and day pupils, allocate proportional whole-number sample sizes, then draw distinct pupils randomly within each category. Rounding needs to preserve the total n and some selected pupils might not respond, so I would check allocations and plan follow-up contacts.
reasoning.tradeoff: Quota sampling can meet targets, but selection within the categories would not be random.

evidence.label: Groups
evidence.text: The study compares boarding and day pupils.

evidence.label: Frame
evidence.text: The complete register identifies each category.

evidence.label: Design
evidence.text: Both groups should appear approximately in their population proportions.

coaching.method: A complete category-labelled frame makes random sampling within boarding/day strata possible.
coaching.reason: Allocate in proportion to group sizes, ensure the whole-number allocations total n, and sample randomly within each.
coaching.limitation: Rounding to whole units may require adjustment, and proportional allocation does not remove nonresponse risk.
coaching.improvement: Check the allocations add to n and plan contacts in each group to address coverage of selected pupils.

method.quota: Quotas can match group totals but generally recruit non-randomly within groups.
method.systematic: A list grouped by boarding status can make a fixed-interval draw risky without checking ordering.

reason.1: Recruiting at a dormitory or gate is not random selection from complete category registers.
reason.2: A fixed interval across a category-sorted list does not guarantee proportional or unbiased selection.

limitation.1: A full register does not guarantee that chosen pupils respond.
limitation.2: Correct proportions for boarding status do not guarantee correct proportions for every other characteristic.

improvement.1: Independent upward rounding can make the total exceed the requested sample size.
improvement.2: The first people available within a category are not the same as random draws.

reasoning.scenario: A factory produces parts in ten-position cycles, with one position always checked by an operator. The inspector needs 30 parts from 300 records and suspects the pattern affects defect rates.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise avoiding alignment with the repeating ten-position production cycle.

reason: Randomly choose 30 distinct numbered parts from a complete frame to avoid locking into one cycle position.
Start systematically at position 1 and choose every tenth part.
Interview the people who packed the parts rather than inspect the parts.
limitation: A simple random sample may still be unbalanced by chance and must be practical to inspect.
Systematic sampling with k=10 is guaranteed to cover every cycle position.
A random sample automatically contains exactly three parts from each cycle position.
improvement: Verify all 300 parts are listed and can be accessed, then draw unique random numbers.
Always choose every tenth item because its interval matches the cycle.
Choose only the end-of-cycle parts.

reasoning.model: I would use a simple random sample of 30 distinct numbered parts from the full set of 300. Taking every tenth item could repeatedly select one phase of the production cycle. Random selection avoids fixing the sample to that phase, although chance variation remains; I would ensure the frame is complete and every selected part can be inspected.
reasoning.tradeoff: A specially designed stratified sample across cycle positions might be stronger if each position needs representation.

evidence.label: Risk
evidence.text: One position in each cycle has already been operator-checked.

coaching.method: A simple random draw from all 300 items avoids fixing the selection to one cycle position.
coaching.reason: Number all parts and select 30 unique labels; a systematic k = 10 scheme risks phase locking.
coaching.limitation: Random draws reduce the cycle-alignment problem, but they do not guarantee exact balance across cycle positions.
coaching.improvement: Verify every part is in the frame and inspect all randomly selected labels to preserve the design.

method.systematic: With interval 10, even a random start can lock every selected unit to one cycle position.
method.opportunity: Surveying packers is not sampling the physical parts whose defects are being studied.

reason.1: Starting at item 1 makes the sample even more tightly tied to one cycle position.
reason.2: Interviews with packers do not constitute inspection of the requested parts.

limitation.1: Sampling every tenth from a ten-position cycle captures one repeated phase, not all ten.
limitation.2: Random sampling does not force exactly three parts from each cycle position.

improvement.1: Matching the interval to the known cycle recreates the selection risk.
improvement.2: Taking end-of-cycle parts only provides no balanced or random coverage.

reasoning.scenario: A researcher wants opinions from all students, including those who study off-site, but the only existing register lists students who attend lessons on campus.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise valid coverage before selecting any sampling method.

reason: First expand the eligibility list to include off-site students, then randomly select distinct units from the completed frame.
Randomly choosing numbers from the campus list automatically includes off-site students.
A larger campus sample compensates exactly for the missing off-site students.
limitation: If off-site students remain missing from the frame, they have no chance of selection.
A bigger sample from an incomplete frame always fixes coverage bias.
Sampling with replacement guarantees no missed subgroup.
improvement: Rebuild and verify the population frame, then contact selected off-site students through suitable channels.
Take a campus-only sample and describe it as all students.
Discard all off-site students from the target population without disclosure.

reasoning.model: I would first construct a full sampling frame covering campus and off-site students, then take a simple random sample using distinct valid numbers. The existing register excludes part of the population, so a random draw from it would not solve coverage bias. I would verify the frame and plan suitable follow-up contact.
reasoning.tradeoff: The design only becomes a genuine random sample of all students after the frame has been repaired.

evidence.label: Population
evidence.text: The target includes campus and off-site students.

evidence.label: Available frame
evidence.text: The only current register covers campus students.

evidence.label: Priority
evidence.text: Coverage must be repaired before generalising.

coaching.method: Random selection is defensible only after constructing a complete frame including off-site students.
coaching.reason: Expanding the list first gives eligible off-site pupils a non-zero chance of selection.
coaching.limitation: Missing frame units have zero chance of selection however random the draw among listed units is.
coaching.improvement: Verify the population register and plan contact for off-site selected students before drawing conclusions.

method.opportunity: Selecting available campus students would exclude off-site students without random inclusion.
method.quota: Quotas would not by themselves repair the missing frame or give off-site students probability of selection.

reason.1: Off-site students absent from the list cannot be chosen by its random labels.
reason.2: Increasing the sample drawn from an incomplete register leaves the excluded group at zero inclusion probability.

limitation.1: A larger sample from the same incomplete frame does not resolve missing units.
limitation.2: Sampling with replacement does not bring omitted members into the frame.

improvement.1: A campus-only sample cannot stand for all students without substantial qualification.
improvement.2: Changing the stated target after seeing a missing group conceals the intended study population.

reasoning.scenario: A town wants to estimate how often residents use parks. Interviewers can work in several parks but cannot obtain a list of every resident. The study must report limitations carefully.
reasoning.priority: Prioritise a practical exploratory survey, without pretending park visitors represent all town residents.

reason: Interview eligible park users who are available, and explicitly limit the strength of conclusions.
A random sample of all residents can be obtained just by choosing one park entrance.
Everyone living in the town is equally likely to be present in a park on Tuesday.
limitation: People who never visit parks could be entirely absent, distorting an estimate for all residents.
There is no possible bias because each person at the park can volunteer.
A convenient sample automatically becomes a census.
improvement: Vary locations/times and state that a resident-wide probability sample would need a better frame.
Interpret the park-user result as a population-wide estimate with no caveat.
Only interview people wearing running clothes.

reasoning.model: An opportunity sample of available park users could provide exploratory information quickly, but it cannot reliably estimate behaviour for every resident because non-users may be excluded. I would sample across several parks and times and clearly label the coverage limitation. A proper resident-wide estimate needs a better sampling design.
reasoning.tradeoff: This is not a strong design for a representative town-wide estimate; feasibility does not justify unwarranted generalisation.

evidence.label: Aim
evidence.text: Explore park usage across residents of the town.

evidence.label: Access
evidence.text: Interviewers can visit several parks but have no resident-wide list.

evidence.label: Missing group
evidence.text: Some residents may never use parks.

coaching.method: Opportunity recruitment at parks is practical for exploratory park-user opinions, not a representative town estimate.
coaching.reason: Recruit reachable park users and restrict claims to what this non-random sample can support.
coaching.limitation: Residents who never visit parks may be entirely absent, making a town-wide estimate unreliable.
coaching.improvement: Different parks and times improve variety, but resident-wide inference needs a better sampling design and frame.

method.stratified: There is no resident-wide frame from which to select random units within defined strata.
method.simple-random: Choosing random park visitors is not a simple random sample of all town residents.

reason.1: One entrance does not provide a resident-wide probability frame.
reason.2: Park attendance varies; many residents cannot be reached there at all.

limitation.1: Volunteering at a park does not remove the exclusion of non-visitors.
limitation.2: Interviewing available park users is not a census of town residents.

improvement.1: A park-user sample cannot support an unqualified town-wide estimate.
improvement.2: Only interviewing runners would further narrow the groups represented.

reasoning.scenario: A school has a complete numbered register of 300 pupils and can survey 30 about journeys to school. It wants an estimate for the whole school, not a particular year group.
reasoning.priority: Use a fair school-wide probability selection without imposing unnecessary subgroup targets.

reason: Number all 300 pupils and use fair random integers to obtain 30 different labels, ignoring repeats.
Interview the first 30 arrivals because every pupil is equally likely to arrive first.
Choose ten pupils from each year group even though year-group sizes are unknown.
limitation: Some randomly selected pupils may refuse, so the responses could differ from the intended random selection.
Random selection ensures all 300 pupils answer even if no reminders are sent.
A sample of 30 is identical to asking all 300 pupils.
improvement: Follow up the original selected pupils and report response rates and limitations before estimating school-wide habits.
Replace any refusal with the selected pupil's closest friend.
Treat the first 30 completed responses as a guaranteed census.

reasoning.model: I would number the complete register and draw 30 distinct random integers, ignoring repeats. This provides a simple random sample of the whole school. Some selected pupils might not reply, so I would follow up and report the response rate rather than claiming perfect representativeness.
reasoning.tradeoff: Stratified sampling might be useful if year-group differences were the purpose, but no group breakdown is needed for this overall estimate.

coaching.method: The available evidence supports simple random sampling: Number all 300 pupils and use fair random integers to obtain 30 different labels, ignoring repeats.
coaching.reason: The justification should use the stated frame and task: Number all 300 pupils and use fair random integers to obtain 30 different labels, ignoring repeats.
coaching.limitation: A genuine risk in this context is: Some randomly selected pupils may refuse, so the responses could differ from the intended random selection.
coaching.improvement: This improvement addresses the named risk: Follow up the original selected pupils and report response rates and limitations before estimating school-wide habits.

method.quota: Quota recruitment would impose fixed group totals but no such targets are needed or supported by group-size data.
method.opportunity: Opportunity recruitment would favour pupils arriving or standing nearby rather than a fair draw from the register.

reason.1: Arrival time is not a fair random-number mechanism for drawing 30 from the full register.
reason.2: Equal group counts require group information and would not necessarily be proportional.

limitation.1: A selected pupil can decline; random selection does not force or guarantee responses.
limitation.2: Thirty observations cannot be the whole population of 300.

improvement.1: Choosing a friend removes the original random mechanism and may add social-selection bias.
improvement.2: A partial responding sample cannot be renamed a complete census.

reasoning.scenario: A factory has 100 numbered safety clips in a batch. Testing a clip to destruction prevents its sale, so inspectors need to test only 10 while treating each clip fairly.
reasoning.priority: Choose ten different clips without destroying the entire batch or favouring a convenient box.

reason: Destroy all 100 clips because a census is always more reliable.
Use a lottery of ten different numbers from 1 to 100 and destructively test the corresponding clips.
Take the ten clips easiest to reach and call them randomly selected.
limitation: A correctly selected sample guarantees that none of the remaining 90 clips is faulty.
Different random sets of ten could contain different defect rates, so the batch estimate has sampling variation.
Without testing every clip it is impossible to obtain any useful information.
improvement: Use only the most accessible clips for better speed and claim the result represents the batch.
Document the random draw and communicate the uncertainty of conclusions from just ten tests.
Increase the test count to 100 regardless of the destructive cost.

reasoning.model: I would select ten different numbers at random from the numbered batch and destroy only those clips in testing. This avoids deliberate selection and preserves most stock, but a defect estimate can vary from one random sample to another. I would report that uncertainty and record the drawing procedure.
reasoning.tradeoff: A census would remove sampling variation but destroy all saleable clips, so it is unacceptable.

coaching.method: The available evidence supports simple random sampling: Use a lottery of ten different numbers from 1 to 100 and destructively test the corresponding clips.
coaching.reason: The justification should use the stated frame and task: Use a lottery of ten different numbers from 1 to 100 and destructively test the corresponding clips.
coaching.limitation: A genuine risk in this context is: Different random sets of ten could contain different defect rates, so the batch estimate has sampling variation.
coaching.improvement: This improvement addresses the named risk: Document the random draw and communicate the uncertainty of conclusions from just ten tests.

method.systematic: Systematic selection would choose positions at a regular interval, not give every ten-clip subset equal chance.
method.quota: Quota selection needs category targets and non-random recruitment; neither is appropriate here.

reason.0: Destroying the whole stock defeats the investigation's stated practical constraint.
reason.2: Choosing the nearest clips is convenience selection, not simple random sampling.

limitation.0: Ten tests cannot prove every untested unit is free of defects.
limitation.2: A sample can inform an estimate even though it cannot guarantee the whole batch.

improvement.0: Taking nearby items reintroduces the location bias the numbered random draw avoids.
improvement.2: A destructive census would leave no saleable clips and is not practical.

reasoning.scenario: A museum has 500 chronologically ordered ticket records and needs to inspect 50 for data-entry errors. The list has no known repeating cycle connected with the errors.
reasoning.priority: Use a quick probability-based rule for evenly spaced positions across the ordered register.

evidence.label: Ordering
evidence.text: No known periodic pattern related to errors

reason: Pick every tenth record starting at position one without any randomisation.
Inspect the first 50 records, as they are fastest to access.
Choose a random start from positions 1–10 and then inspect every tenth record.
limitation: A random starting position guarantees the selected records cover every possible pattern.
Spacing selections evenly makes every possible 50-record sample equally likely.
If the register contains an unnoticed ten-record cycle, the fixed interval could distort the selected records.
improvement: Remove the random start so the same records are always checked.
Discard records in the middle of the list to speed up inspection.
Inspect the list for periodic ordering and change or randomise the ordering if a relevant pattern is found.

reasoning.model: I would choose one of positions 1 to 10 at random and then take every tenth ticket record to make 50. This is quick across the complete list. I would check for periodic patterns because a ten-record cycle could distort the result, even with a random start.
reasoning.tradeoff: Simple random sampling is defensible but requires many separate draws; systematic sampling is easier to administer here.

coaching.method: The available evidence supports systematic sampling: Choose a random start from positions 1–10 and then inspect every tenth record.
coaching.reason: The justification should use the stated frame and task: Choose a random start from positions 1–10 and then inspect every tenth record.
coaching.limitation: A genuine risk in this context is: If the register contains an unnoticed ten-record cycle, the fixed interval could distort the selected records.
coaching.improvement: This improvement addresses the named risk: Inspect the list for periodic ordering and change or randomise the ordering if a relevant pattern is found.

method.simple-random: A simple random sample uses individual chance draws rather than the required easy fixed-interval inspection.
method.opportunity: Opportunity selection of the first available records would overrepresent one part of this chronological register.

reason.0: Beginning deterministically is an incomplete systematic random procedure.
reason.1: Taking the earliest records alone offers no planned coverage across the full list.

limitation.0: A random start does not neutralise a period-ten cycle in the data.
limitation.1: Systematic selection restricts possible subsets; it is not a simple random sample.

improvement.0: Omitting randomness makes selection less defensible, not more.
improvement.1: Skipping the middle defeats the aim of covering the whole record list.

reasoning.scenario: A boarding school has 240 boarders and 160 day pupils. Researchers need a sample of 40 to compare homework travel arrangements across the two groups. Complete lists are available.
reasoning.priority: Keep the two boarding categories proportionally represented and select pupils randomly inside each.

reason: Select 24 boarders and 16 day pupils randomly from the two complete group registers.
Approach any 24 boarders and 16 day pupils near the canteen, without random draws.
Choose 20 from each group because there are two groups.
limitation: Differential nonresponse by boarders and day pupils could distort the final comparison.
Matching the planned 24:16 split guarantees everyone selected will respond.
Using separate registers means all sampled homework habits will be identical.
improvement: Follow up selected nonrespondents in both groups and report response rates separately.
Replace refusing boarders with their closest roommates.
Discard the smaller day-pupil group from the analysis.

reasoning.model: I would make two strata, allocate 24 places to boarders and 16 to day pupils, and randomly select those pupils from the separate registers. Nonresponse may still affect the realised sample, so I would follow up and compare response rates for both groups.
reasoning.tradeoff: Quota sampling could achieve fixed counts without complete registers, but it would lose the available within-group random selection.

coaching.method: The available evidence supports stratified sampling: Select 24 boarders and 16 day pupils randomly from the two complete group registers.
coaching.reason: The justification should use the stated frame and task: Select 24 boarders and 16 day pupils randomly from the two complete group registers.
coaching.limitation: A genuine risk in this context is: Differential nonresponse by boarders and day pupils could distort the final comparison.
coaching.improvement: This improvement addresses the named risk: Follow up selected nonrespondents in both groups and report response rates separately.

method.quota: Quota sampling matches targets but uses non-random recruitment within the groups.
method.simple-random: One simple random draw could leave unpredictable representation of the smaller day-pupil group.

reason.1: Approaching convenient pupils makes this quota, not stratified random selection.
reason.2: Equal 20:20 counts misrepresent the actual 60:40 population split.

limitation.1: Selection proportions do not force responses, so response composition can differ.
limitation.2: Different pupils can have widely different homework and travel arrangements.

improvement.1: Roommate substitution introduces convenience and social-network effects.
improvement.2: Removing day pupils prevents the stated comparison altogether.

reasoning.scenario: An event organiser has no full visitor register but wants 12 weekday and 8 weekend visitors to comment on a new booking system. Interviewers can recruit willing visitors on site.
reasoning.priority: Fill the requested group targets without pretending a probability frame exists.

reason: Allocate 12 and 8 places but claim people were randomly selected from nonexistent registers.
Invite willing visitors within each group and stop when its stated target is filled.
Survey any 20 visitors regardless of which day they attended.
limitation: Meeting the two targets guarantees accurate representation of every age and booking preference.
Within each quota, people available and willing to speak may differ from other visitors.
Quota sampling automatically makes every possible twenty-person sample equally likely.
improvement: Call the sample stratified because the two totals were fixed.
Recruit at varied times, record refusals where feasible, and state the non-random selection limitation.
Only interview the friendliest weekday visitors to save time.

reasoning.model: I would use quota sampling, approaching available volunteers until there are 12 weekday and 8 weekend visitors. This respects the requested groups without a complete frame. Willing people may differ from those unavailable, so I would sample at several times and explain that limitation.
reasoning.tradeoff: Opportunity sampling is quicker but does not guarantee the organiser's weekday/weekend totals.

coaching.method: The available evidence supports quota sampling: Invite willing visitors within each group and stop when its stated target is filled.
coaching.reason: The justification should use the stated frame and task: Invite willing visitors within each group and stop when its stated target is filled.
coaching.limitation: A genuine risk in this context is: Within each quota, people available and willing to speak may differ from other visitors.
coaching.improvement: This improvement addresses the named risk: Recruit at varied times, record refusals where feasible, and state the non-random selection limitation.

method.stratified: Stratified random sampling would require actual random selection within each group, not on-site volunteering.
method.simple-random: Simple random sampling from all visitors cannot be carried out with no usable population frame.

reason.0: Targets alone do not make a non-random recruitment process into probability sampling.
reason.2: Ignoring weekday/weekend totals would not satisfy the specified group composition.

limitation.0: A quota on day type does not balance every other characteristic or willingness to participate.
limitation.2: Quota sampling does not satisfy the defining equal-subset probability of simple random sampling.

improvement.0: Changing the label does not change how respondents were selected.
improvement.2: Selecting only friendly volunteers increases rather than reduces convenience bias.

reasoning.scenario: A council wants feedback from 30 renters and 20 homeowners. It has broad population estimates but cannot obtain household names; a small team can visit several public sites.
reasoning.priority: Achieve the requested tenure-group numbers using available respondents and be explicit about non-random recruitment.

reason: Interview the first 50 people encountered with no check on housing type.
Choose every fifth household from a list the council does not possess.
Ask eligible volunteers at several sites and stop recruiting each housing group at its target.
limitation: Once 30 renters reply, every renter in the council area has an equal chance of inclusion.
Survey totals exactly matching two groups prove that the results are unbiased.
People who visit these sites and agree to respond may not represent others in the same housing group.
improvement: Treat the totals as random draws because the group counts look plausible.
Ignore group targets if one housing category proves hard to recruit.
Vary sites and times, monitor both quotas and report how convenience-based recruitment limits inference.

reasoning.model: I would recruit volunteers to fill the 30 renter and 20 homeowner quotas at several locations. This guarantees the requested category counts but not a random sample of either group. I would vary recruitment times and acknowledge that people absent from the sites may hold different views.
reasoning.tradeoff: Stratified random sampling would be preferable with complete tenure lists but those lists are unavailable.

coaching.method: The available evidence supports quota sampling: Ask eligible volunteers at several sites and stop recruiting each housing group at its target.
coaching.reason: The justification should use the stated frame and task: Ask eligible volunteers at several sites and stop recruiting each housing group at its target.
coaching.limitation: A genuine risk in this context is: People who visit these sites and agree to respond may not represent others in the same housing group.
coaching.improvement: This improvement addresses the named risk: Vary sites and times, monitor both quotas and report how convenience-based recruitment limits inference.

method.systematic: Systematic sampling needs an ordered frame and random start, neither of which is available.
method.opportunity: Opportunity sampling alone does not enforce the explicit 30:20 group totals.

reason.0: Uncontrolled convenience recruitment could omit a required tenure group.
reason.1: The missing list prevents a valid interval-based household selection.

limitation.0: Volunteer recruitment does not give every renter a known or equal inclusion chance.
limitation.1: Filling one demographic margin does not remove self-selection bias.

improvement.0: Renaming volunteer recruitment does not make it a probability draw.
improvement.1: Dropping the quotas defeats the council's stated coverage objective.

reasoning.scenario: A cafeteria manager wants quick initial feedback on a new kiosk from people who actually use it today. The aim is exploratory; no claim is needed about all school pupils.
reasoning.priority: Collect practical feedback from immediately available kiosk users, recognising its limited scope.

evidence.label: Claim
evidence.text: Not an estimate of all pupils

reason: Ask willing kiosk users available during the day and state that the results describe this convenient group.
Invent age quotas so the exploratory task can be labelled stratified.
Claim all school pupils have an equal inclusion chance because the kiosk is open.
limitation: Pupils who did not visit the kiosk today may have different views or needs.
Since the question is exploratory, an opportunity sample cannot have any limitations.
The sample is a census of all pupils as long as every kiosk user agrees.
improvement: Gather feedback over several days and keep conclusions about kiosk users rather than the whole school.
Report the results as exact population percentages for all school pupils.
Invite only people who praised the kiosk to maximise positive feedback.

reasoning.model: I would ask willing kiosk users who are available today for initial feedback. This opportunity sample is fast but cannot describe pupils who did not use the kiosk. I would collect responses on other days and keep my conclusions limited to the kiosk-user group.
reasoning.tradeoff: A school-wide random survey could support general conclusions but is unnecessary for an immediate pilot among current kiosk users.

coaching.method: The available evidence supports opportunity sampling: Ask willing kiosk users available during the day and state that the results describe this convenient group.
coaching.reason: The justification should use the stated frame and task: Ask willing kiosk users available during the day and state that the results describe this convenient group.
coaching.limitation: A genuine risk in this context is: Pupils who did not visit the kiosk today may have different views or needs.
coaching.improvement: This improvement addresses the named risk: Gather feedback over several days and keep conclusions about kiosk users rather than the whole school.

method.quota: Quota sampling would require explicit subgroup targets not needed for this exploratory user-feedback task.
method.simple-random: Simple random selection requires a full frame and does not match the immediate kiosk-user access.

reason.1: Inventing groups does not turn convenient participants into a random stratified sample.
reason.2: Opening the kiosk to everyone does not mean everyone attends or is sampled.

limitation.1: Exploratory aims still require explaining whom the findings might omit.
limitation.2: Even a census of kiosk users is not a census of every pupil.

improvement.1: Convenience percentages do not support unrestricted population estimates.
improvement.2: Selective recruitment of enthusiastic users makes feedback less balanced.
